query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In equiatomic CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, when X is aluminum, the alloy (in an initially single-phase homogeneous solid-solution state) will form, under isothermal exposure at >900 °C in an oxidative atmosphere, a continuous, coherent, and slow-growing Al2O3-rich oxide scale that remains adherent and resists cracking and spallation over prolonged exposure (e.g., 100 hours); conversely, when X is manganese or silicon, more rapid outward cation diffusion leads to formation of heterogeneous, porous oxide scales prone to cracking.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CrFeCoNiX alloys (with X = Al, Mn, or Si) in a well-annealed single-phase solid solution (and optionally a multiphase variant as a secondary test) prepared by standard arc melting and homogenization.
generation.intervention: Expose polished specimens to a controlled oxidative atmosphere (e.g., air with controlled oxygen partial pressure) at temperatures above 900 °C (e.g., 920–950 °C) for durations up to 100 hours.
generation.conditions: Temperature >900 °C, isothermal oxidation in dry air (or corrosive atmosphere if desired), with controlled exposure times (e.g., 1, 24, 50, and 100 hours); baseline comparison with an alloy lacking X substitution (i.e. conventional CrFeCoNi).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, continuous, Al2O3-rich sub-scale at the alloy surface which acts as a barrier to further cation diffusion and oxygen ingress, maintaining mechanical coherence.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum’s lower diffusivity and higher thermodynamic stability in forming Al2O3 (compared with Mn or Si-based oxides) drives preferential outward diffusion to form a dense, adherent oxide layer. This protective oxide limits further diffusion of both metal cations and oxygen, thereby mitigating internal stresses that would otherwise lead to cracking or spallation. In contrast, alloys with X = Mn or Si are expected to exhibit greater cation mobility and form more mixed, porous oxide scales due to faster diffusion kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: For the Al-containing alloy, post-exposure analyses (e.g., cross-sectional SEM, TEM, and XRD) will reveal a continuous, coherent, and slow-growing Al2O3-rich oxide layer with minimal cracking/spallation and lower overall mass gain (indicative of protective behavior) compared to the baseline and Mn/Si-containing alloys. In contrast, Mn- and Si-containing alloys will display thicker, heterogeneous oxide scales with evidence of cracking and spallation.
generation.baseline: An equiatomic CrFeCoNi alloy without any X substitution, expected to form non-protective oxide scales with moderate to high oxide growth and spallation at >900 °C.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is valid for alloys processed into single-phase solid solutions with uniform microstructure; deviations (e.g., multiphase bonding boundaries, porosity introduced by processing) may alter diffusion kinetics and oxide stability. The test is specific to oxidative or corrosive atmospheres at temperatures above 900 °C and exposure durations up to ~100 hours.
generation.uncertainty: Variations in local microstructural features (e.g., grain size and presence of secondary phases) may affect oxide adherence. Additionally, the precise kinetics of cation versus oxygen diffusion, especially in multiphase states, may introduce variability that must be carefully controlled. Also, there is some conflicting evidence regarding the behavior of chromium-rich versus aluminum-rich oxides in different atmospheric conditions (see PMC8346963).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of equiatomic CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Al, Mn, and Si, along with a control alloy without X. Polished specimens are to be oxidized in a dry air atmosphere at 930 °C for 100 hours. Use cross-sectional SEM, TEM, and high-resolution XRD to characterize the oxide scale structure, thickness, and phase composition. Measure mass gain curves and perform spallation tests (e.g., repeated thermal cycling) to assess oxide adherence.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity from cross-sectional SEM/TEM
Phase identification (Al2O3, Mn-oxides, SiO2, Cr2O3) via XRD
Spallation or cracking incidence via surface roughness and microstructural examination
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not produce a continuous, adherent, and slow-growing Al2O3-rich oxide scale (i.e. it exhibits similar oxide discontinuities, cracking, or spallation as the Mn- or Si-containing alloys) or if the baseline (CrFeCoNi) exhibits equally good oxidation protection, then the hypothesis that aluminum substitution uniquely governs the formation of a stable protective oxide at >900 °C is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: At temperatures exceeding 500 °C, the oxidation behavior of traditional and complex alloys (e.g., Ni-Cr, Ni-based superalloys, Fe-Cr, CoCrFeNiMn ‘Cantor’ alloy) has been extensively studied in oxygen-rich environments and over extended periods (from days to hundreds of days,). Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. The presence of Mn, known for its high mobility and low-energy oxide formation, can deplete Mn in the alloy, causing pore formation and accelerating oxide growth. Tradition

The oxidation behavior of Cr-Mn-Fe-Co HEA produced by 3D laser printing was investigated at 700 °C and 900 °C up to 48 h. The main conclusions are as follows: (1) The initial alloy was verified as FCC random solid solution. The mass gain in the oxidation process for 48 h was measured to be 0.02 and 0.15 g/cm2 at 700 °C and 900 °C, respectively. (2) MnFe2O4, MnFeO2 and Cr2O3 were detected by the XRD analysis on the specimen surface. Some surface cracks were observed, especially for those oxidized at 900 °C. The spallation of oxide layer took place when the alloy was tested at 900 °C. The high-temperature oxidation resistance of the alloy sharply decreased when the test temperature increased from 700 °C to 900 °C, leading to the wide application under 700 °C.

AbstractThe equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy prepared by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering underwent partial substitution of Mn by Al (5, 10 and 15 at.%) to determine its influence on mechanical properties and thermal stability. It was discovered that the higher the Al content, the higher the volume fraction of the hard phase with primitive cubic (PC) crystallographic lattice, which increases the hardness and strength of the alloys. The most promising mechanical properties have been achieved in the CoCrFeNiMn5Al15 alloy reaching the compressive yield strength (CYS) of 2135 ± 21 MPa and the ultimate compressive strength (UCS) of 2496 ± 21 MPa. All the prepared alloys showed good thermal stability as they maintained or only slightly reduced their initial hardness during the 100 h annealing at 800 °C. Furthermore, the higher the Al content, the higher the resistance against high-temperature oxidation. papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Model equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy (a proxy system for CrFeCoNiX alloys) subjected to oxidation in controlled oxygen environments
papers.approach: In situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure to track early oxidation stages and subsequent evolution of surface oxides
papers.findings: Initial oxidation follows trends based on atomic size and redox potential. A layered oxide develops with compositional inversion over time where elements like Cr preferentially form oxide, while Mn tends to segregate toward outer layers under prolonged exposure at high temperature.
papers.mechanism: Interplay between preferential elemental oxidation (governed by redox potential and cohesive energy) and Fickian diffusion results in a gradual, speciation-driven hierarchical oxide structure; controlling the relative outward cation flux and inward oxygen diffusion appears to be key to forming a continuous protective scale.

papers.title: High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co HEA (closely related to CrFeCoNiX systems, especially when considering Mn substitution effects)
papers.approach: 3D laser printing to prepare HEA samples followed by isothermal oxidation tests at 700 °C and 900 °C, with XRD and cross-sectional microstructural analysis
papers.findings: At 700 °C a relatively adherent, though imperfect oxide is formed; at 900 °C, extensive cracking, porosity, and spallation occur along with phase segregation into Mn-rich spinels and Cr2O3, which fails to provide a long‐term protective barrier.
papers.mechanism: Kinetic mismatch between the rapid outward diffusion of species (particularly when Mn is present) and the slower inward oxygen diffusion leads to heterogeneous oxide layers that become mechanically unstable and prone to spallation.

papers.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA with tailored ultrafine-grain microstructure
papers.approach: Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to study oxidation kinetics over temperature ranges 850–1050 °C; microstructural and oxide scale characterization
papers.findings: Processed ultrafine-grained samples exhibited lower mass gain and reduced oxidation kinetics compared to as-cast samples. The formation of a dense, thin oxide barrier (rich in Cr and Al oxides) is correlated with increased activation energies for oxidation.
papers.mechanism: Enhanced grain boundary diffusion in ultrafine structures facilitates the rapid formation of a stable, adherent oxide scale that limits further oxidation via a diffusion‐controlled mechanism.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Insights into the Oxidation Mechanisms of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Using In Situ X-ray Diffraction.
papers.system: CrMnFeCoNi HEA exposed to high temperatures (up to 1100 °C) in air
papers.approach: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) to monitor phase appearance/disappearance and oxide scale evolution as temperature increases
papers.findings: A graded oxide scale develops: initial formation of Mn2O3 at lower temperatures that later transforms into mixed oxides such as Mn3O4 and MnCr2O4. The evolving oxide structure reflects the differential diffusion of Mn, Cr, and Fe as temperature increases.
papers.mechanism: Thermodynamic and kinetic competition among multiple elements leads to temperature-dependent phase transformations in the oxide scale; the relative diffusion rates (Mn > Cr > Fe) set the stage for a non-uniform oxide structure that may or may not become protective.

papers.title: Influence of the Al Content on the Properties of Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X HEAs with partial substitution of Mn with Al
papers.approach: Mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering, with oxidation tests conducted at 800 °C to assess weight gain kinetics and oxide scale formation
papers.findings: Increased Al content led to a shift in the surface oxide composition from Mn-oxides to Al-based oxides. Alloys with higher Al showed logarithmic oxidation kinetics indicating the formation of a dense, protective scale with improved high-temperature oxidation resistance.
papers.mechanism: Aluminum promotes the formation of stable Al2O3 scales which, due to lower growth rates and better adherence, act as effective diffusion barriers; this contrasts with the unstable, volatile oxides formed when Mn dominates the surface reactions.

papers.title: An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide.
papers.system: Refractory high entropy alloy similar to CrMoTiAlY systems with modified Ti content
papers.approach: Isothermal oxidation studies via thermogravimetric analysis at 1000 °C and 1100 °C, complemented by microstructural and elemental mapping analyses
papers.findings: At 1100 °C, formation of a continuous, dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer was observed, which limited further oxidation and provided a barrier against oxygen ingress. Reduced Ti content appeared to favor this CrTaO4 formation.
papers.mechanism: A stable and coherent CrTaO4 layer develops through controlled outward cation diffusion and limited oxygen ingress, effectively sealing the substrate. The formation kinetics and elemental partitioning (e.g. lower Ti favoring CrTaO4) are critical in maintaining layer integrity.

established: Oxidation kinetics in high-entropy alloys are primarily diffusion controlled, following parabolic or logarithmic laws.
Protective oxide layers, particularly those rich in Al2O3 or Cr-based oxides, are associated with improved oxidation resistance.
Elemental diffusion rates (e.g., Mn diffusing faster than Cr and Fe) play a critical role in the formation and stability of the oxide scale.

approaches_tried.approach: Varying alloy composition (e.g. substituting Mn with Al)
approaches_tried.outcome: Higher Al content leads to the formation of dense, protective Al2O3 scales and improved oxidation resistance at high temperature.
Enhanced grain boundary diffusion promotes rapid formation of stable, thin oxide layers that slow down further oxidation.

approaches_tried.approach: Controlled in situ high-temperature XRD and thermodynamic modeling
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed temperature-dependent phase changes in the oxide scales and the influence of differential diffusion of alloy constituents.

mechanisms: Diffusion control: Outward diffusion of metal cations versus inward oxygen diffusion determines oxide growth.
Element-specific oxidation: Differences in redox potentials and diffusion rates (e.g., Mn vs Cr vs Al) lead to layered oxide formation.
Protective scale formation: Establishment of slow-growing, coherent oxide films (e.g., Al2O3, CrTaO4) that act as effective barriers.
disagreements: Some studies indicate that chromium-rich oxides (Cr2O3) are unstable above 900 °C due to volatility (formation of CrO3), while others emphasize the role of chromium in forming protective barriers.
The relative contributions of kinetic factors (e.g., grain boundary versus lattice diffusion) versus thermodynamic driving forces in oxide layer stabilization remain debated.
open_questions: What are the precise conditions (composition, temperature, exposure time) under which the transition from a protective, coherent oxide scale to a cracked/spalled layer occurs?
How do minor alloying elements (Si, Mn, or Al in CrFeCoNiX) quantitatively alter the balance between cation and oxygen diffusion rates?
What is the role of the multiphase versus single-phase solid-solution state in the long-term stability of the protective oxide?
opportunities: Perform controlled baseline experiments on CrFeCoNi alloys with single-phase and multiphase states and systematically vary X (Si, Mn, or Al) to directly correlate composition with oxide scale integrity.
Leverage in situ high-temperature characterization (e.g., HTXRD, microscopic imaging) over long durations (>100 h) to capture real-time evolution of oxide formation at >900 °C.
Combine thermodynamic modeling with experimental diffusion studies to develop a unified mechanistic hypothesis that links elemental partitioning to oxide layer adhesion and mechanical stability.
Investigate processing techniques (e.g., grain refinement) alongside compositional modifications to understand interfacial adhesion and mitigate spallation.

directions.direction: Alloy composition design by varying the minor element X (Si, Mn, or Al) to promote formation of different protective oxides (e.g., Al2O3 versus Mn‐rich spinels or silica) via selective elemental oxidation.
directions.assessment: This direction directly addresses the problem by testing how the identity of X affects the oxide‐scale chemistry. Prior work (e.g. PMC9692591 and PMC11169556) shows that increasing Al tends to form dense, protective Al2O3 scales, while Mn often leads to faster outward cation diffusion and unstable oxide layers. The physics and thermodynamics of selective oxidation are well established, and composition can be controlled precisely. This approach is highly feasible and results would be directly informative regarding stability.

directions.direction: Microstructure control through processing to obtain a single-phase homogeneous versus multiphase solid-solution state.
directions.assessment: Changes in microstructure, such as grain size and phase homogeneity, can affect diffusion pathways and stress development in the oxide scale. Evidence from ultrafine-grain studies (PMC9026100) supports that refined microstructures can enhance protective oxide formation. However, it may not isolate the influence of X itself and introduces extra variables.

directions.direction: Thermomechanical treatment (e.g., pre-oxidation or controlled surface deformation) to adjust cation diffusivity and residual stresses at the metal/oxide interface.
directions.assessment: By modifying the kinetics of cation diffusion and the adhesion of the oxide, this method could promote cohesive oxide layer formation. However, while it is feasible, it adds complexity in decoupling processing effects from intrinsic compositional effects and may mask the role of X.

directions.direction: In situ high-temperature characterization (using HTXRD or in situ TEM) to monitor real-time phase evolution in the oxide layer.
directions.assessment: This approach yields direct insight into the kinetics of oxide phase formation and transformations above 900 °C. Although it can reveal the mechanistic pathways, it is more observational rather than an intervention designed to control the outcome, and thus less direct for isolating the effect of X.

directions.direction: Modeling and simulation of diffusion and oxidation kinetics in multi-component HEAs to predict flux balance of cations vs oxygen.
directions.assessment: Computational studies can help predict whether a slow-growing, coherent oxide will form by simulating differential diffusion rates and thermodynamic stability. While supportive, modeling alone does not constitute a direct experimental test and usually requires validation from experiments.

choice.direction: Alloy composition design by varying the minor element X to promote selective formation of a protective oxide scale.
choice.why: This direction directly addresses the mechanistic question by isolating the effect of adding Al, Mn, or Si into the CrFeCoNi matrix. Prior evidence strongly suggests that high Al content promotes formation of a coherent, slow-growing Al2O3 layer (PMC9692591, PMC11169556) while Mn leads to faster diffusion and defective scales (PMC8346963). It is experimentally feasible and allows a controlled comparison against a baseline alloy without X, facilitating a clear, falsifiable mechanism regarding the role of differential cation diffusion and oxide stability above 900 °C.
